sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Xōlōtl** ​(*xolotl*) — ‌The Twin ‌Who Leads ​the ​Sun — ​belongs to ​the Nahuatl ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Evening Star, ‌Death, Twins". ​The ‌name means ​"The double, ​the monster"[^1].

​Xōlōtl ​is the ​twin who ‌goes down ​with ‌the sun: ​brother of ‌Quetzalcōātl, guide ​of ‌the dead ​across the ‌underworld's river, ​and ​the god ‌who turned ‌himself ‌into maize, ​maguey, and ​finally the ‌axolotl ​rather than ​be sacrificed. ‌He is ​the ​Aztec soul's ‌ferryman — ​and the ‌lake ​that still ​bears his ​name.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the name ‌as **Xōlōtl** ​and serves ‌its ​temple at ​[xōlōtl.com](https://xn--xltl-l3ab.com). The ‌restoration ‌preserves distinctive ‌features the ‌ASCII form ​loses ‌— the ​macrons on ​ō marking ​the ‌long vowels ​— which ​places the ​name ‌in Tier ​1. The ​plain ASCII ​form ‌*xolotl* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation survives ‌for ​this name; ​**Xōlōtl** is ​a ​scholarly transliteration ​of the ‌reconstructed ​spoken form. ​Etymologically the ‌name means ​"The ‌double, the ​monster"[^1].

The ‌ASCII ​form *xolotl* ​survives only ​because ​the early ​domain-name system ‌could ​not carry ‌diacritics; it ​is ‌a technological ​compromise, not ‌an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ​**Xōlōtl** recovers ‌the vowel ‌length of ‌the ​original directly ​in the ‌address ​bar. The ​restoration preserves ‌distinctive ​features the ​ASCII form ‌loses ​— the ‌macrons on ​ō ​marking the ​long vowels ​— ‌which places ‌the name ​in ‌Tier 1.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- ‌**x** → ‌**X** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**o** → ​**ō** ​— Long ​vowel
- ‌**l** ​→ **l** ​— Same
​- ‌**o** → ​**ō** — ​Long ​vowel
- ‌**t** → ​**t** ‌— Same
​- **l** ‌→ **l** ​— ‌Same

The ‌project holds ​the ​domain **xōlōtl.com** ​(xn--xltl-l3ab.com) as ​the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/ˈʃoː.loːtɬ/** — ​Classical ​Nahuatl.[^1]

‌For ​the modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​SHOH-lotl, ‌long ​ō ​on both ​syllables.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical forms ​of ‌the ​name:

‌- **Nahuatl** ​— ‌Xōlōtl
​- ‌**His animal** ​— ​axolotl
‌- ‌**Owned form** ‌— ​Xōlōtl

​Xōlōtl ‌carries two ​long ​ō ‌vowels, ​both preserved ​in ‌the ​restoration; ‌the final ​-tl ​is ​Nahuatl's ​signature consonant ‌cluster, ‌released ​laterally ‌— the ​sound ​every ‌visitor ‌learns on ‌the ‌name ​of ‌the water-monster, ​the ​axolotl, ​that ‌shares his ​name ​and, ​in ‌myth, his ​skin. ​The ​final ‌-tl is ​Nahuatl's ‌lateral ​affricate, ‌released to ​the ‌side ‌of ​the tongue ​— ​the ​sound ‌that ends ‌axolotl ​too.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous ‌writing system ‌is ​securely ​attested ​for ​individual nahuatl ​names. ‌The ​form ​shown ‌is a ​modern ‌scholarly ​transliteration.[^1]

‌The form ​**Xōlōtl** ​is ​therefore ​a ​scholarly transliteration ‌rather ​than ‌an ​attested ancient ‌spelling; ​it ‌encodes ​the ‌reconstructed sound ​of ​the ‌name ‌for ‌modern use, ​and ​no ‌mark ​in it ​is ‌decorative.

​The ​codices ‌write him ​as ‌what ​he ​is: ​the dog-headed ​god, ‌often ‌shown ​twisted in ‌transformation ​— ​half ‌into ‌maize, half ‌into ‌the ​water-beast ‌— ​with the ​twin's ​ball-court ‌and ​the Venus ​star ​in ‌his ​glyphic ​entourage. The ​name ‌and ​the ‌animal (xōlōtl, ​"water ‌monster," ​the ‌axolotl) ‌are one ​word: ​the ​god ​hiding ‌inside his ‌own ​spelling.

sources.citation: Florentine Codex (General History of the Things of New Spain), Bernardino de Sahagún; School of American Research, 1577.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Xōlōtl ​is the ‌twin ‌who ​goes down ​with ​the sun: ​brother ​of ‌Quetzalcōātl, guide ​of ​the ‌dead across ​the ‌underworld's river, ​and ‌the ​god who ​turned ​himself into ​maize, ​maguey, ‌and finally ​the ‌axolotl ​rather than ‌be ​sacrificed. He ‌is ​the ‌Aztec soul's ​ferryman ​— and ‌the ‌lake ‌that still ​bears ​his ‌name.[^1]

### ​The ​Dog

His ‌animal: ​the ​guide that ‌leads ​the dead ‌across ​the ​ninefold river ​of ​Mictlān.

### ‌The ‌Evening ​Star

Venus ‌at ​dusk ​— his ‌station, ‌twin to ‌his ‌brother's ​morning star.

‌### ​The Axolotl

​His ​final ‌disguise: the ​water-monster ​of ​Xochimilco, gilled ‌and ​smiling, that ​shares ​his ‌name.

### ​The ‌Empty Sockets

​The ‌codices ​show him ‌weeping ‌his ​eyes out ​at ​the gods' ​sacrifice ‌— ‌grief itself, ​dog-eared.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Xōlōtl's myths ​run on twoness: twin ‌of the morning star, ‌guide of the dying ​sun, the god who ​is always the second ​of a pair — ​and always the one ​who goes down into ‌the dark.[^1]

### Across ​the Nine Waters (The ​Guide)

The Aztec dead ‌journeyed four years through ​Mictlān's nine levels, and ‌at the deep river ​it was the dog ‌— Xōlōtl's creature — ​who swam them across; ​a soul whose family ​had mistreated dogs in ​life found no ferryman. ​The funeral rite buried ‌a red dog ​with the dead: the ‌god's own form, sacrificed ​to carry its master ‌home. Among the world's ​psychopomps, he is the ‌only one who comes ​as a pet.[^2]

### ‌The God Who Hid ​(The Sacrifice)

At the ​creation of the fifth ‌sun the gods gathered ‌at Teotihuacan to sacrifice ‌themselves and set the ​new sun moving. Xōlōtl ​refused to die: he ‌fled, weeping so hard ​his eyes fell from ​their sockets, and hid ‌— as the twin-stalked ​maize, as the doubled ​maguey, and at last ‌as the axolotl ​in the lake. They ‌found him even there, ​and he died like ​the rest: the myth ​of the price of ​survival, and of the ‌god who begged to ‌live and serves death ​anyway.

### Venus Split ‌in Two (The Twins)

​Quetzalcōātl is Venus as ​morning star, herald of ‌the light; Xōlōtl is ‌Venus as evening star, ‌which follows the sun ‌into darkness. The astronomy ​is exact — one ‌planet, two appearances — ​and the myth makes ​it biography: one twin ​leads the dawn out ‌of the night, ​the other escorts the ​day into it. Together ​they keep the star's ‌whole circuit, and the ​world's whole hope.

### ​The Bones of the ​Fathers (The Descent)

When ‌the fifth age needed ​people, Quetzalcōātl descended to ‌Mictlān for the bones ​of the dead — ‌and Xōlōtl went with ​him as guide through ‌the underworld's traps. The ‌bones, ground and sprinkled ​with the gods' own ​blood, became humankind: every ​Aztec child was thus ​made of the dead, ‌carried up by the ‌dog-god's knowledge of the ​road back.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The ​friars ‌identified him ‌with ​the ​devil's ​lesser ​angels, but ​the ‌people ​kept ​him closer ‌to ​a ‌saint ​of the ‌road: ​the ​dog ​that ​guards the ​grave ‌and ​guides ‌the traveller ​survived ‌in ​Mexican ‌folk ​custom, and ‌the ​hairless ​xoloitzcuintli ‌— the ‌national ‌dog, ​named ​from his ‌name ​— ​was ‌never ​exorcised. Scholars ​pair ‌him ​with ‌every underworld ​canine ​from ​Cerberus ​to ‌Anubis, and ‌the ​Maya ‌twins' ​underworld journey ​in ‌the ‌Popol ‌Vuh runs ‌on ​his ‌same ​road. ​The axolotl, ​his ‌water-form, ​became ​Mexico's ambassador-species: ​the ‌smiling ​face ​of ​conservation itself.[^1]

‌Within ​the ‌Nahuatl ​tradition, closely ‌related ​names ‌in ‌the corpus ​include ​[[cihuacoatl|Cihuacōātl]], ​[[coatlicue|Cōātlīcue]], ​[[huitzilopochtli|Huitzilopōchtli]], ‌[[itzpapalotl|Itzpapālōtl]], [[mictlantecutli|Mictlāntēcutli]], ‌and ​[[quetzalcoatl|Quetzalcōātl]].

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Xōlōtl ​is the ‌god ‌of the ​way through. ​He ​did not ​want ​the job ‌— he ​wept, ​hid, and ‌transformed ​to escape ‌it ​— and ‌he does ​it ​still: the ​sun ​into the ​dark, ‌the dead ​across the ‌river, ​the lost ‌back ​home. He ‌asks the ​guide's ‌question, which ​is ​also the ‌mourner's: ‌who walks ‌with you ​into ​the night ‌— ​and whom, ​in ‌your turn, ​will you ​guide?

‌The axolotl's ​refusal ‌to grow ​up — ​keeping ​its gills, ​its ‌larval smile, ‌its ​power to ‌regrow a ​heart ​— has ‌made ‌it the ‌scientist's ‌darling and ​the city's ‌emblem, ​and it ​is ​the god's ‌final joke: ​the ​deity who ​begged ‌not to ​die ​survives as ​the animal ‌that ​regenerates everything. ‌Xōlōtl's ​question is ‌the ​guide's own: ‌transformation is ‌not ​escape — ​but ​sometimes, in ​the last ‌lake, ‌it is ​enough.[^1]
